Dear Sam

> 1. As far as I know, sleep efficiency = SleepDurationInSpt / SptDuration;

The widely accepted calculation is time in bed divided by the total duration of sleep after sleep onset. This is why GGIR does not report sleep efficiency in part 4 output if you do not have a sleep diary that asks about time in bed and argument sleepwindowType = "SPT" (default). However, sometimes researchers use your equation,  for example when time in bed is not known. This is why I included it only in part 5 and not in the part 4 output. Maybe the documentation on this can be a bit clearer.

> I wonder how SleepDurationInSpt is calculated? If I want to calculate SleepDurationInSpt can I find these elements in part4 or part5 table?

It is the sum of all sustained inactivity bouts that overlap with the guider, this cannot be derived from other variables in the csv report, but is derived inside GGIR. However, if you export the time series you would be able to verify the calculation.

> Is this window guider_SptDuration used to define the period of time the subject is in bed, and if so, what is the meaning :(SleepDurationInSpt / guider_SptDuration )?

Hopefully my first answer above clarifies this.

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Javier,

Cut-points derived from raw data accelerometry are mostly applicable across sensor brands. When there are multiple cut-points available for an age group I would recommend trying to use an average of multiple studies or to stick with the cut-point used in other studies you want to compare with.

Note that it is your responsibility as a research to choose the cut-points. We or GGIR cannot do that for you: The choice depends on your knowledge of your the study protocol, the study population, and the way you plan to interpret your results.

Best, Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Dear Clair,

> Would specifying includedaycrit=10 in one round of data processing and includedaycrit = 16 in another round matter in terms of output?
​

Argument includedaycrit specifies the number of valid hours in a day that are required.

If all your days have less than 10 or more than 16 hours the output should be the same.
If some days have more than 10 and less than 16 hours you would expect that some days are omitted from the day summary results, and not taken into account in the person (recording) level averages.

Regards,

Vincent

messages.subject_clean: Activity report problem and Graphical issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Francesco,

Below some answers to your questions, hope they help.

Visual report
Note that the visual report generated by GGIR (barplots and behavioral classification) is intended only for a quick impression of the data and does not reflect all the information that you get in the csv reports. The MVPA barplot is showing 0 minutes in every day, and this reflect the time accumulated in MVPA in the longest bout duration that you defined (i.e., 10 minutes in your function call). You can get a more detailed look at the time in activities in the part 5 csv reports.

Naps
GGIR is not optimized for naps detection for now. GGIR facilitates nap detection based on a model that was trained in 3-year-olds, so I do not think this is applicable to your population. If  you use this algorithm (see arguments below), then you should get two variables in part 5 daysummary/personsummary reports (i.e., nap_totalduration and nap_number).

Report example colors
These plots are stored in meta/sleep.qc folder and they are generated by default in GGIR.

Note that GGIR is an open-source software which is developed driven by the community efforts/needs. If you want to help improve the visualizations, nap algorithms, or any other functionality of GGIR, we are happy to discuss the options.

Best,
Jairo

Hi Iris,

I think you can use outpoints in cpm as in ActiLife.

Dear Ya Li,
I think you are matching data from part 4 and part 5. The comparison is not always straitforward as you might allow criteria in part 5 that are different than part 4 (such as the guider).
It is better to compare data at individual basis using night and day summary to understand the data. In part 5 data are examined in minutes and in part 4 in hours so the rounding might lead to small differences.

 Sleep state is based on absence of rotation of the wrist of more than 5° for at least 5 min (or 10 min depending on your criteria) that overlap with the sleep window (if your algorithm is based on a sleep log)
If no sleep log used, there is another algorithm to define sleep onset and waking time

Inactivity is defined as acceleration < 40 mg (or different cut point)

In part 5, dur_spt_sleep_min is the timing asleep (defined as no rotation from the wrist of more than 5° for at least 5min) during the sleep window (between sleep onset and waking)

 dur_spt_wake_IN_min is the time inactive (defined as acceleration < 40 mg or 30mg depending on your criteria) when awake during the sleep window.

so we don't expect  dur_spt_sleep_min  to be the same as  dur_spt_wake_IN_min
Best wishes,
Séverine Sabia

Hi Iris,

> Thanks for responding. I tested this but If have some additional questions.
>
> So if I want to use the cut-point from Sasaki et al. (Freedson V3) than the following cut-points are proposed:
> Lpa <2690,
> MPA 2691-6166,
> VPA > 6166
>
> These cut-points were established at 60 sec epochs at 30 hz wearing the Actigraph on the hip.
> As I work with Actigraphs worn on the hip and I use 60 sec epochs at 100 hz. I think I need to convert these values?
> I recorded at 6000 data points per epoch (60sec x 100 hz)
> Sasaki recorded at 1800 datapoints per epoch (60 sec x 30 hz)
> So do I need to cutpoint/60*18 ?
> LPA< 807 cpm
> MPA 808-1849 cpm
> VPA: >1949 cpm.

You should not incorporate the sample rate difference, because this is already accounted in the count calculation. Instead, only look at epoch length, which is identical if you use 60 second epochs. So, I think no correction is needed if cut-points in ActiLife are used at 60 second epoch level. If you would use 5 second epoch in GGIR then the correction would be to divide by 12 (or multiple by 0.08333).

> 1) But with these cutpoints we do not have a SB-LPA treshhold which we need to define in GGIR to distinguish LPA from SB. Most cpm are using 100 or 150 cpm to define the threshold form SB to LPA however, these were calculated for vertical axis devices and not for vector magnitude. Do you have any suggestions how to define this cut-point?
> When using the above mentioned cut points - I get a potential underestimation of MVPA then when I check I manually with Actilife.

do.neishabouricounts = TRUE
acc.metric = "NeishabouriCount_y"

Hi Elif and Ben,

This information is all stored inside the meta/ms2.out RData files. I only implemented the functionality epochvalues2csv = TRUE for those with limited R skills.

A better solution may be to document the format of those files and provide some guidance on how to use those files. That said, it took me under 5 minutes to write the following code which essentially derives the time series you are looking for:

# Load content of RData file from meta/ms2.out folder is loaded in R.
load("output_test/meta/ms2.out/01_left wrist_012345_2000-01-01 12-45-78.bin.RData")

# Convert timestamp to POSIX for convenience
tsFormat = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"
tz = ""
IMP$metashort$timestampPOSIX = as.POSIXlt(IMP$metashort$timestamp, format = tsFormat, tz = tz)

# Interpolate scores as they are in a different resolution
shortEpochLength = IMP$windowsizes[1]
longEpochLength = IMP$windowsizes[2]
NlongInsideShort = longEpochLength / shortEpochLength
scores = IMP$rout[rep(1:nrow(IMP$rout), each = NlongInsideShort),]

# Add column names to clarify what is what
colnames(scores) = c("nonwear", "clipping", "additonal_nonwear", "studyprotocol", "all")

# Now combine the scores with the epoch level timeseries
IMP$metashort = cbind(IMP$metashort, scores)

# IMP$metashort now be stored or used for your own R project work
write.csv(x = IMP$metashort, file = "myfile.csv", row.names = FALSE)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Christoph,

Whether you can "trust" GGIR depends on your understanding of what GGIR does, your ability to tailor GGIR to your study protocol and research needs, and the extent to which you account for all this when interpreting the results.

To help you with this we provide documentation <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html> on what GGIR can do with references to literature, we provide a list of possible cut-points <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/CutPoints.html> that you may want to consider, we offer training <https://www.accelting.com/ggir-training/> courses on how to use GGIR, and I/we can provide support with specific questions/problems here in the google group or as paid consultancy.

In my opinion the term 'validated' is overrated in this field. Many of the 'gold standards' come with significant limitations themselves, and true 'validity' in the field heavily depends on how a method is used and interpreted. Methodological research is important to help understand a method and its limitations, but should not be seen as a certificate to justify unlimited use in research.

Best regards,

Vincent

messages.subject: Re: epoched sleep/wake time series
messages.body_plain:
Hi Eva,

If your protocol instructed participants to only wear accelerometers during nighttime, then I would say that part 5 reports are not informative for you as GGIR would only provide sleep-related outcomes (part 4 reports).

Part 5 classifies valid and invalid days based on the argument "includedaycrit.part5 <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIRParameters.html#:~:text=when%20strategy%20=%201.-,includedaycrit.part5,or%20as%20the%20number%20of%20hours%20in%20a%2024%20hour%20day.,-excludefirstlast.part5>", which is 2/3 by default (requiring 2/3 of the waking time to be valid to include that day). Also, by default, part 5 timeseries would skip the invalid days, see argument "save_ms5raw_without_invalid <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIRParameters.html#:~:text=if%20save_ms5rawlevels%20=%20TRUE.-,save_ms5raw_without_invalid,from%20the%20time%20series%20output%20files.%20Only%20used%20if%20save_ms5rawlevels%20=%20TRUE.,-storefolderstructure>" which is TRUE as default. Then, I think GGIR is not storing the SPTs in the timeseries because all your days are being classified as invalid. I guess that you can fix that by setting "save_ms5raw_without_invalid = FALSE" and/or setting "includedaycrit.part5 = 0", but I have never tried this.

Hope this helps!

Best,
Jairo

messages.body_plain:
Hi Christian and Ben,

Epochs do not start on the hour. They are aligned with the nearest start of a long epoch  which in turn are align with the hour. The long epoch length is by default is 15 minutes. 13:12 becomes 13:15 and 13:27 becomes 13:30, etc.

This is done intentional to standardise epoch alignment relative to the day across individuals and across days. Aligning it with the start of a recording would not be logical.

Note that this has been discussed previously: https://groups.google.com/g/rpackageggir/c/qUU4-fQmhxw/m/K6MMO3cYAwAJ and in various other threads.

So, to get a resolution closer to the start of the recording you could set windowsizes to c(5, 60, 3600), the second value of which defines the epoch length in seconds.

Also see this <https://epochvalues2csv> recent thread where I explained that the exporting to csv is in itself a redundant functionality as all info is also stored in the RData file.

Thanks,

Vincent

messages.subject: Re: Inactivity GGIR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yasmine,

According to the widely accepted definition of sedentary behaviour (See table 5, Tremblay et al, https://ijbnpa.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12966-017-0525-8#ref-CR25), it is done in a "sitting, reclining or lying posture". I'm assuming your participants wore the Axivity on the wrist, therefore there will be no way of determining what posture the participant is in - therefore the terminology is inactive time from GGIR because some of that inactive time likely includes behaviours such as standing.

Though there will be a large crossover between inactive and sedentary time, the terminology is important as the 2 behaviours are different, particularly from the perspective of a sedentary behaviour researcher - hence why monitors are generally worn on the thigh where sedentary behaviour is of particular interest (e.g. Axivity on the thigh as done in ProPASS, and the activPAL worn on the thigh).

Thanks,
Ben

Hi Christian,

Reading in csv is not going to work as ActiGraph seems to have changed their csv file format for this new service and GGIR only knows how to deal with one ActiGraph csv file format.

If gt3x file is not available the best next option is then to use GGIR's functionality to read ad-hoc csv file formats as you did: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/readmyacccsv.html
The header you are trying to read does not meet the header criteria, so you will need to skip those arguments for header extraction.

See here our unit-test that demonstrate how it can handle headers:https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/tests/testthat/test_read.myacc.csv.R

I think with the following
you are nearly there:

GGIR(rmc.firstrow.acc = 8,

rmc.col.acc = c(2, 3, 4),
rmc.col.time = 1,

the main thing that seems to be going wrong in your last error is the timestamp recognition.

Can you try to go back to  read.myacc.csv() and explore the specification of the timestamp format and timezone until that function produces a clear POSIX class column. Note that this functionality has improved in the recent 2.9-0 release, so maybe update GGIR is part of the trick.

Best regards,
Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Yasmine,

In addition to Ben's response: Keep in mind that these definitions of sedentary behaviour are only words. What matters most is whether the methods we use truly capture the behaviour these words describe.

In my personal opinion "sedentary behaviour" has been defined in an unfeasible way. Some methods such as thigh worn sensors may be good at capturing the sitting/reclining aspect of it but it is questionable whether those methods can capture the <1.5 MET criteria consistently in the real world as humans can work with their arms that involves more than 1.5 MET of energy expenditure while sitting. Also thigh worn data has the major flow that it is not good at distinguishing sleep as the posture is identical to sitting on a chair for a while. Similarly, other methods such as wrist or hip worn sensors may be good at capturing the 1.5 MET-criteria but fail at capturing the posture criteria.

So, for that reason I have tried to avoid using the term "sedentary behaviour" in the GGIR documentation. Although, maybe it is good to have a reflection like this in the documentation somewhere as this is not the first time someone asks about it. That said, most studies who have used GGIR in the context of sedentary behaviour research then referred to their data as sedentary behaviour estimates.

A better solution would be to update the definition of sedentary behaviour to something that we can realistically measure and for which clearly defined gold standards exist.
See also my reflections on physical activity measurement, which suffers form the same poor construct definition: https://www.accelting.com/updates/how-to-measure-pa-guideline-adherence/

Best,

Vincent
